note: What a real triage model answered for every comment US-029 labelled by hand, plus PLAN.md's four worked example posts. `triage-examples.test.ts` replays these. The two numbers that decide the stage are here: how many people asking it kept, and how many people answering it dropped, which is the saving. A kept count below the total is not automatically a fault: the hand label says whether a person is asking, and triage is asked whether they are a person to reach, which is a different question. Two threads and 46 comments is not a distribution.

monitor.product: A test runner for web apps. You record a browser flow once and it keeps working when the UI changes.
monitor.idealCustomer: Small SaaS teams, two to twenty people, with no dedicated QA engineer, shipping every week.
monitor.problem: End-to-end tests break whenever the UI changes, so teams stop trusting them and go back to testing by hand before every release.

item.title: Starting Automation from 0% as a QA Lead — How are you using AI, MCPs & Agents in QA?
item.excerpt:
I’d put all my early energy into locator strategy and test data management, those two things will cause more headaches than any flaky test later on. Playwright’s got decent built-in locators but if you’re leaning on AI for generation you’ll want a strict naming convention or data attributes from the start, otherwise the AI will just latch onto fragile selectors and you’ll spend half your week fixing tests.

 For MCPs the Playwright one is obvious but hooking into your database for test data setup/teardown is where it really shines, you can prompt Claude to spin up a fresh account with specific flags and tear it down after the run without writing a ton of boilerplate. Agents for failure analysis are still mostly hype in my experience, they’ll confidently tell you a test failed because of a timeout when it was actually a bad selector, but they’re surprisingly useful for churning out repetitive spec files once you’ve got a solid template locked in.

item.title: Starting Automation from 0% as a QA Lead — How are you using AI, MCPs & Agents in QA?
item.excerpt:
Focus on wherever the weak spots are with the current manual test suites per Fintech app/system under test and help whoever has developed those first, then use the tools available to help you draft a test plan including an automation development/implementation plan - ensure you get buy-in from product team/s and do research based on the infra/system/platform/app contexts, designs and requirements of your Fintech test targets.
Once you've developed automated (or even just semi-automated) unit test scripts locally on your dev machine, use agentic IDEs like Claude Code to help you build out your test suites in your CI pipeline. I've had success with setting up both Gitea and Forgejo Actions and runners in my homelab for personal projects which has helped me to understand Gitlab runners as part of my day job - but your team may use other tools. Basically, each time you commit and merge/push test code changes to your repo it can triggers your CI suite to run a set of automated functional API/unit tests, plus more E2E tests with Playwright (I'm using Python version as my codebase is mostly Python/Flask based) but quite often you'll need to work with developers and DevOps colleagues on how to 'hand over' fully/successfully validated code for promotion from dev/test to later environments.

item.title: Playwright is significantly better than Selenium.
item.excerpt:
Personally, I don't like the fact that Playwright doesn't have the option of running tests on real Safari

 .

 WebKit

 is not the same as real Safari. It's like saying Edge, Chrome and Brave are identical because they use chromium, and yet everyone has seen bugs that only appear on one of them.

 I work at the software department of a major global airline, we can't risk not running regression tests on actual Safari, since a certain percentage of the paying users are on that browser.

 We were using Selenium until 2 years ago, and we never had any "flaky" situations, because we knew how to add waits correctly (without being wasteful). We were very happy with it.

 But the department director wanted us to move to one of those "smart AI" testing tools, we did a long POC, it turned out ok, and here we are.

 I miss writing Selenium code, but the upside is that now more devs and testers are contributing to the tests.

 If I were to change jobs and go to a smaller company that doesn't give a crap if their customers can't use their product on Safari, I'd be happy to work with Playwright.

Ultimately playwright is a Microsoft hack with lots of limitations: WebKit and not safari, browsers tied to playwright versions causing a lag, emulated mobile (not even simulated FFS) amongst others.

 Playwright is hobby grade useful for noobs and startups where quality is an after thought.

 Ultimately if you prefer playwright over selenium it's a skill issue. Hell I'd even go with selenium just because BiDi is w3c.
